title: Between two opinions (1 Kings 18:21–39)
hookLine: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" on Mount Carmel

cards: Mount Carmel, and the slope is full of people. King Ahab has sent for all the children of Israel, and they've come up to watch a contest. On one side stand the prophets of Baal, the god Queen Jezebel favors.

On the other stands one man: Elijah. The land has had no rain for a long time. Before any fire is lit, before any altar is built, Elijah turns, not to the king and not to the prophets, but to the people watching.
And he asks them a question.

teach.b: In the King James words: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" To halt, in old English, is to limp: someone hobbling, one foot on each side of a fork in the road, never quite walking down either.
Then Elijah finishes the thought: if the Lord be God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him. The text gives the crowd's reply.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE ANSWERED NOT A WORD.
teach.b: The people answered him not a word. Nobody wants to choose. Then the contest.
Two altars, two bulls, no fire; whoever answers with fire is God. The prophets of Baal call out from morning until noon, and there was no voice, nor any that answered.
Elijah rebuilds a broken altar of the Lord, has water poured over it until the trench runs full, and prays a short prayer. Fire falls and consumes everything, even the water in the trench.

teach.h: THE LORD, HE IS THE GOD.
teach.b: And the people who said not a word fall on their faces: "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God." But the question came before the fire. Elijah was after an end to the limping.
In Jewish practice, the people's cry from this chapter returns at the very end of Yom Kippur, called out by the whole congregation as the gates of the day close.
A people that once could not answer at all now answers together. The story keeps the uncomfortable middle part, too: the long silence, the people waiting to see who would win before they spoke.
It doesn't pretend that choosing is easy. It only asks how long.

how: Jews read the contest on Mount Carmel as a haftarah, and at the close of Yom Kippur the congregation calls out the people's words from this chapter, that the Lord is God.

games.q: you're in the crowd on Mount Carmel. Elijah asks how long you will limp between two opinions. what does the crowd do?
o: shout out for the Lord at once.
games.why: the people answered him not a word. only after the fire falls do they cry out, the Lord, he is the God.

practice: Find the thing you've been limping on, one foot on each side: a call you keep almost making, a habit you keep almost dropping, a yes or a no left hanging, and notice what the waiting has cost.
Then, quietly, let one side land, without acting on it yet, the way the people's silence finally turned into words. If you pray, you can ask for clarity.

wordCard.voice: Halt. The old word for limping, what Elijah said the people were doing between two opinions. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: how long between two opinions. Standing at the fork has its own cost. Until tomorrow.
